column1: In SQL Server JSON path expressions, {{c1::$}} denotes the document root.
column2:
Add a path step after the root to select something inside the document. For example, $.id selects a root-level property.
DECLARE @j nvarchar(max) = N'{"customer":{"name":"Ada"},"items":[{"product":"Book"}]}';
SELECT JSON_VALUE(@j, '$.customer.name') AS CustomerName;
Review source

column1: To extract the scalar name inside customer, use JSON_VALUE(@j, '{{c1::$.customer.name}}').
column2:
The path enters the customer object before reading name. It does not find every property with that name.
DECLARE @j nvarchar(max) = N'{"customer":{"name":"Ada"},"items":[{"product":"Book"}]}';
SELECT JSON_VALUE(@j, '$.customer.name') AS CustomerName;
Review source

column1: The first items element's product uses JSON path '$.items[{{c1::0}}].product'.
column2:
Index 0 selects the first array member. The final path step then reads product from that member.
DECLARE @j nvarchar(max) = N'{"customer":{"name":"Ada"},"items":[{"product":"Book"}]}';
SELECT JSON_VALUE(@j, '$.items[0].product') AS Product;
Review source

column1: SQL Server JSON_VALUE uses {{c1::lax}} path mode by default.
column2:
Omitting the path mode uses lax. Specify strict when a missing path must raise an error instead.
DECLARE @j nvarchar(max) = N'{"id":1}';
SELECT JSON_VALUE(@j, '$.price') AS Price; -- NULL (lax)
Review source

column1: To make a missing price property raise an error, use JSON_VALUE(@j, '{{c1::strict}} $.price').
column2:
The prefix changes how the missing path is handled. It does not change the stored JSON document.
DECLARE @j nvarchar(max) = N'{"id":1}';
SELECT JSON_VALUE(@j, 'strict $.price'); -- Missing path raises an error.
Review source

column1: Define a typed OPENJSON result with OPENJSON(@j) {{c1::WITH}} (Price DECIMAL(10,2) '$.price').
column2:
WITH defines the output column type and the source path. The declared DECIMAL type converts the matching scalar.
DECLARE @j nvarchar(max) = N'{"id":1,"price":12.50}';
SELECT ProductID, Price
FROM OPENJSON(@j)
WITH (ProductID int '$.id', Price decimal(10,2) '$.price');
Review source

column1: Map JSON property id to a differently named column with OPENJSON(@j) WITH (ProductID INT {{c1::'$.id'}}).
column2:
ProductID is the output name and $.id is the source path. They do not have to use the same name.
DECLARE @j nvarchar(max) = N'{"id":1,"price":12.50}';
SELECT ProductID, Price
FROM OPENJSON(@j)
WITH (ProductID int '$.id', Price decimal(10,2) '$.price');
Review source

column1: Preserve a nested items array with OPENJSON(@j) WITH (Items NVARCHAR(MAX) '$.items' {{c1::AS JSON}}).
column2:
AS JSON keeps the array as a JSON fragment. It is not a request to convert all items into separate SQL rows.
DECLARE @j nvarchar(max) = N'{"customer":{"name":"Ada"},"items":[{"product":"Book"}]}';
SELECT Items FROM OPENJSON(@j)
WITH (Items nvarchar(max) '$.items' AS JSON);
Review source

column1: In SQL Server 2022+, JSON_OBJECT({{c1::'id':ProductID}}) creates an id property from ProductID.
column2:
The string before the colon becomes the name of the property. The expression after it supplies the value.
-- SQL Server 2022+
SELECT JSON_OBJECT('id': ProductID) AS ProductJson
FROM dbo.Products;
Review source

column1: SQL Server 2022+ builds the array of supplied strings with {{c1::JSON_ARRAY}}('sql','azure').
column2:
This constructor builds an array directly from the two input expressions. It does not combine several query rows.
-- SQL Server 2022+
SELECT JSON_ARRAY('sql', 'azure') AS Tags;
Review source

column1: SQL Server 2022+ nests customer data with JSON_OBJECT('customer':{{c1::JSON_OBJECT('id':CustomerID)}}).
column2:
The inner call produces the id object, and the outer call puts that object under customer.
-- SQL Server 2022+
SELECT JSON_OBJECT('customer': JSON_OBJECT('id': CustomerID))
FROM dbo.Customers;
Review source

column1: In SQL Server, JSON_ARRAYAGG was introduced in {{c1::2025}}.
column2:
SQL Server 2022 has scalar JSON constructors, but that does not give it this row aggregate.
Review source

column1: In SQL Server 2025, sort aggregated array elements with JSON_ARRAYAGG(OrderID {{c1::ORDER BY OrderID}}).
column2:
The ordering inside the function determines the positions of elements. An outer ORDER BY would sort result rows instead.
-- SQL Server 2025
SELECT CustomerID, JSON_ARRAYAGG(OrderID ORDER BY OrderID) AS Orders
FROM dbo.Orders
GROUP BY CustomerID;
Review source

column1: SQL Server 2025 JSON_ARRAYAGG defaults to {{c1::ABSENT ON NULL}} for SQL NULL inputs.
column2:
The default skips SQL NULL values. Request NULL ON NULL when the output needs an explicit JSON null in their place.
-- SQL Server 2025
SELECT JSON_ARRAYAGG(Value) AS DefaultArray,
       JSON_ARRAYAGG(Value NULL ON NULL) AS IncludeNull
FROM (VALUES (1), (NULL)) AS v(Value);
Review source

column1: In SQL Server 2025, search native-json @j for tag sql using JSON_CONTAINS(@j,{{c1::'sql'}},'$.tags[*]').
column2:
Pass the value sql as a SQL string. Extra literal quotation marks would change the value being searched for.
-- SQL Server 2025
DECLARE @j json = '{"tags":["sql","azure"]}';
SELECT JSON_CONTAINS(@j, 'sql', '$.tags[*]') AS HasSql;
Review source

column1: In SQL Server 2025, search a tags array in native-json @j with JSON_CONTAINS(@j,'sql',{{c1::'$.tags[*]'}}).
column2:
The wildcard selects the array's elements at that path. The search compares the supplied SQL value against them.
-- SQL Server 2025
DECLARE @j json = '{"tags":["sql","azure"]}';
SELECT JSON_CONTAINS(@j, 'sql', '$.tags[*]') AS HasSql;
Review source

column1: Expose a JSON category as a computed column with ALTER TABLE Products ADD ProductCategory AS {{c1::JSON_VALUE(ProductData,'$.category')}}.
column2:
The expression extracts the property when SQL Server needs the computed value. The column can be indexed if it meets the index requirements.
ALTER TABLE dbo.Products
ADD ProductCategory AS JSON_VALUE(ProductData, '$.category');
Review source

column1: Store the base-table value of a suitable JSON computed column by adding {{c1::PERSISTED}} to its definition.
column2:
PERSISTED stores and maintains the value in the base row. That differs from storing it only as a key in an index.
ALTER TABLE dbo.Products
ADD ProductCategory AS CAST(JSON_VALUE(ProductData, '$.category') AS nvarchar(100)) PERSISTED;
Review source

column1: For NVARCHAR JSON, extract a numeric price with {{c1::CAST(JSON_VALUE(@j,'$.price') AS DECIMAL(10,2))}}.
column2:
JSON_VALUE alone returns text in this example. The cast lets downstream arithmetic use a decimal value if the text is convertible.
DECLARE @j nvarchar(max) = N'{"price":12.50}';
SELECT CAST(JSON_VALUE(@j, '$.price') AS decimal(10,2)) AS Price;
Review source

column1: SQL Server shapes nested JSON with column aliases using FOR JSON {{c1::PATH}}.
column2:
PATH uses the column aliases to shape the result. A dotted alias can put a property inside a nested object.
SELECT ProductID AS 'product.id', ProductName AS 'product.name'
FROM dbo.Products
FOR JSON PATH;
Review source

column1: Wrap FOR JSON PATH output under a products property with FOR JSON PATH, {{c1::ROOT('products')}}.
column2:
The wrapper contains one property called products. The value of that property is the array produced by the query.
SELECT ProductID AS id FROM dbo.Products
FOR JSON PATH, ROOT('products');
Review source

column1: A nested id under product uses SELECT ProductID AS {{c1::'product.id'}} FROM Products FOR JSON PATH.
column2:
The alias puts id inside the product object. It does not rename the SQL source column.
SELECT ProductID AS 'product.id', ProductName AS 'product.name'
FROM dbo.Products
FOR JSON PATH;
Review source
